node.title: Krebs cycle connection to electron transport
node.canonical_question: How does the Krebs cycle supply electrons to the transport chain?
node.summary: Each acetyl-CoA through the Krebs cycle yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, and 1 GTP. These carriers feed the electron transport chain.

seeds.question: How do NADH and FADH2 donate their electrons to the transport chain complexes?
Why does FADH2 yield less ATP than NADH?
What happens to the GTP produced in the Krebs cycle?

parsed.rendering_md:
The TCA cycle (also called the Krebs cycle) does not pass electrons directly to the electron transport chain. Instead, it loads high-energy electrons onto two carrier molecules.

**NADH** is the main carrier. Each turn of the cycle produces 3 NADH molecules. NADH carries its electrons to Complex I of the transport chain.

**FADH2** is the second carrier. Each turn produces 1 FADH2. It delivers electrons at Complex II, which is a step further down the chain than Complex I.

Because FADH2 enters at a later point, it drives fewer proton pumps than NADH does, so it ultimately generates less ATP.

The cycle also makes 1 GTP per turn (in some cells this is ATP directly), but GTP is not an electron carrier - it is used directly as an energy currency.

In total, one glucose molecule produces two acetyl-CoA molecules, so the Krebs cycle turns twice per glucose, yielding 6 NADH and 2 FADH2 from the cycle itself. These carriers then feed their electrons into the electron transport chain to drive most of the cell's ATP production.
